faq.q: What is the bedside test for cryptococcal meningitis?

faq.a: Fluconazole has better oral bioavailability, fewer drug interactions, and is widely available in low‑resource settings.
faq.q: Why is fluconazole preferred over itraconazole for oral thrush?

exam: A 35‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with headache and papilledema – what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a rapid CrAg test; a positive result confirms cryptococcal meningitis and guides urgent antifungal therapy.

A child with severe malnutrition has oral white plaques and low‑grade fever – how do you differentiate simple thrush from invasive candidiasis? — Look for systemic signs (persistent fever, tachycardia, hypotension) and obtain blood cultures; isolated oral thrush without systemic signs is treated locally.

In a farmer with fever, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly, what key history points point toward histoplasmosis? — Exposure to bird or bat droppings, soil work, and immunosuppression; these raise suspicion for endemic dimorphic fungus.

Why is amphotericin B preferred for induction therapy in cryptococcal meningitis despite its toxicity? — It achieves rapid fungicidal activity and reduces mortality; toxicity is managed with hydration and electrolyte monitoring.

A patient on rifampicin develops disseminated candidiasis – which antifungal should be avoided and why? — Itraconazole should be avoided because rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, markedly lowering itraconazole levels.

How would you manage a suspected dermatophyte infection when microscopy is unavailable? — Base treatment on clinical appearance (ring‑shaped, scaly lesions) and start topical terbinafine or oral fluconazole if extensive.
What are the red‑flag signs that a superficial fungal infection may be masking a deeper problem? — Persistent fever, lymphadenopathy, weight loss, or immunosuppression suggest systemic involvement.

When is it acceptable to use oral fluconazole alone for cryptococcal meningitis? — In settings where amphotericin B is unavailable and the patient has mild to moderate disease; high‑dose fluconazole is given with close monitoring.
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Covers common pathogenic fungi encountered in East African hospitals, their transmission, clinical presentation, diagnosis without advanced labs, and pragmatic management.

b: Common agents: Candida spp., Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei, dermatophytes, and endemic dimorphic fungi.
High‑risk groups: HIV/AIDS, malnutrition, diabetes, chronic lung disease, and patients on steroids.
sections.p: Fungal infections range from superficial skin disease to life‑threatening systemic mycoses. In low‑resource settings, limited diagnostics and co‑morbidities such as HIV shape presentation and outcomes.

b: Candida – budding yeast, pseudohyphae on KOH.
Cryptococcus – encapsulated yeast, India ink positive.
Histoplasma – small intracellular yeast, grows on Sabouraud agar.
sections.p: Fungi are eukaryotic, have cell walls of glucan and chitin, reproduce by spores (sexual and asexual). Dimorphic fungi exist as molds in the environment and yeast in tissue.

b: Inhalation → pulmonary focus → dissemination (esp. in immunosuppressed).
Skin breach → dermatophytes or Candida cutaneous infection.
sections.p: Most infections are acquired by inhalation of spores or direct contact with contaminated skin/mucosa. Endemic dimorphic fungi live in soil; exposure is occupational or recreational.

b: Candida: oropharyngeal thrush, esophagitis, invasive candidemia.
Cryptococcus: meningitis with headache, neck stiffness, papilledema.
Histoplasma: fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia.
sections.p: Clinical syndromes vary by organism and host immunity. Key presentations in East Africa include oral thrush, esophageal candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated histoplasmosis, and chronic dermatophytosis.
Laboratory capacity is often limited; bedside clues and simple tests guide therapy.

t.a: KOH wet mount of skin scrapings
t.b: Detects fungal hyphae → confirms dermatophyte or Candida infection.
Shows encapsulated yeast → points to cryptococcal meningitis; if unavailable, consider rapid antigen lateral flow assay.

t.a: Serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) lateral flow test
t.b: Positive result confirms cryptococcal disease; can be done on finger‑stick blood.
Growth indicates candidemia; if culture not possible, treat empirically in septic patients with risk factors.
Diffuse reticulonodular pattern suggests pulmonary histoplasmosis; if X‑ray unavailable, rely on clinical triad of fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly.

b: Fluconazole – first‑line for oral thrush, esophageal candidiasis, and cryptococcal meningitis induction (if amphotericin unavailable).
Amphotericin B deoxycholate – preferred for severe cryptococcal meningitis and disseminated histoplasmosis; monitor renal function.
Itraconazole – step‑down for histoplasmosis after induction; avoid in patients on rifampicin.
Terbinafine – for dermatophyte infections; safe in pregnancy.
sections.p: Therapy combines antifungal agents with management of underlying conditions. Drug choice reflects availability, toxicity, and interactions.

b: In an HIV patient with headache, consider cryptococcal meningitis; do CrAg LFA even if CSF unavailable.
Oral thrush in a malnourished child signals possible systemic candidiasis; start fluconazole while awaiting cultures.
Diffuse hepatosplenomegaly + pancytopenia in a farmer suggests disseminated histoplasmosis; treat with amphotericin B if possible.
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, risk‑factor assessment, and pragmatic investigations.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening mental status or seizures (possible meningitis)
Severe sepsis with hypotension in a patient on antifungal therapy
Acute renal failure after amphotericin B initiation
